subject: Climate & Environment
title: Composting and Organic Recycling
description: A fast breakdown of Composting and Organic Recycling for builders.

hook.text: Food scraps and yard waste make up over 30% of what we throw away. All of it is compostable.

buildup.text: Composting turns organic waste into nutrient-rich soil that helps plants grow.

discovery.text: It also prevents methane emissions that would occur if the same waste rotted in a landfill.

twist.text: San Francisco mandates composting for every household and business. It diverts 80% of waste from landfill.

climax.text: Home composting is simple. Even small apartments can use indoor worm bins for food scraps.

punchline.text: Trash becomes soil. Waste becomes food. The cycle is right there.

quiz.question: What percentage of household waste is organic and compostable?

details.summary: Composting converts food scraps, yard waste, and other organic matter into nutrient-rich soil amendment through controlled biological decomposition. It diverts waste from landfills, eliminates methane emissions from anaerobic decay, and produces a product that enriches soil and helps retain water.
details.whyItMatters: Organic waste is the largest component of landfill by weight and the primary source of landfill methane. Composting is a proven, scalable solution with immediate climate benefits.
takeaways: Composting prevents methane that organic waste would produce in landfills
The finished product enriches soil and improves water retention
Organics are the largest category of landfilled waste by weight

faq.question: What can be composted?
faq.answer: Food scraps, yard trimmings, coffee grounds, eggshells, paper towels, and cardboard can all be composted. Meat and dairy can be composted in industrial facilities that reach high temperatures but are usually avoided in home composting due to odor and pest concerns.

faq.question: How does composting reduce greenhouse gas emissions?
faq.answer: In landfills, organic matter decomposes without oxygen, producing methane. Composting provides oxygen so microbes produce CO2 instead, which is 80 times less potent as a greenhouse gas. The resulting compost also sequesters some carbon in soil.
